questions.question: Why does USP ⟨1660⟩ describe the appearance of glass lamellae as a "lagging indicator"?

options.A: Because lamellae form only after the drug product has passed its expiry date, so they can serve only as a retrospective record
options.B: Because delamination is the final stage of the glass corrosion reaction, so by the time it is observed it can no longer be addressed by preventive measures
options.C: Because lamellae adhere to the inner container surface before filling and can be detected only after a water rinse
options.D: Because lamellae are always smaller than 50 µm and hard to see with the naked eye, so they can only be confirmed afterwards with instruments

questions.explanation: Delamination lamellae indicate a strong interaction between the drug product and the inner glass surface; they represent the final stage of a complex glass corrosion reaction, and by the time they are visible they can no longer be prevented. Lamellae range from <50 µm to 200 µm, so they are not always smaller than 50 µm, and they do not form only after expiry.

questions.question: Compared with soda-lime-silica glass, what benefit does boron provide in borosilicate glass?

options.A: It raises the coefficient of thermal expansion (COE), making the glass easier to work at high-temperature forming, while also lowering surface alkali content
options.B: It lowers the connectivity of the glass network so that surface ions leach out more easily, which makes them easier to remove later by water rinsing
options.C: It increases the sodium and potassium oxide content, giving the glass higher chemical durability than all other glass types
options.D: It lowers the COE to increase thermal shock resistance and raises network connectivity to increase resistance to hydrolytic attack

questions.explanation: The presence of boron lowers the COE, so the glass is more resistant to thermal shock, and it increases the connectivity of the glass network, so it is more resistant to hydrolytic attack. Soda-lime-silica glass has the higher COE (80-90 × 10^-7) and is the type prone to breaking from thermal shock.

questions.question: A product requires a large glass vial of more than 100 mL. According to USP ⟨1660⟩, how are such containers usually produced, and why?

options.A: By molding, because it is technically very difficult to make tubing with a diameter large enough to produce vials above 100 mL
options.B: By two-step conversion of glass tubing, because molded glass cannot achieve the volume uniformity required for large vials
options.C: By flame forming from glass tubing, because molded glass can only use a Type III formulation
options.D: By molding followed by ammonium sulfate treatment, because large vials must have a silica-rich inner surface

questions.explanation: Molded vials are made in a one-step process (molten glass is cut into a gob and formed in a mold). It is technically very difficult to produce tubing of sufficiently large diameter, so vials above 100 mL are produced by molding. The reasons given in the other options are not found in the text.
questions.reference: USP ⟨1660⟩ Formation of Molded and Tubular Glass Containers

questions.question: After forming, containers pass through an annealing furnace (lehr), where they are heated to 20° to 30° above the transition temperature (Tg) and then cooled slowly. What is the purpose and importance of this step?

options.A: To remove surface alkali ions; if omitted, the pH shift of the container increases but mechanical strength is not affected
options.B: To fuse the container base to the neck; if omitted, the container shows appearance defects such as stones
options.C: To relieve stresses created during forming; poorly annealed containers have reduced chemical and mechanical durability
options.D: To induce phase separation in the glass to improve homogeneity; if omitted, alkali borates on the inner surface volatilize

questions.explanation: Annealing is a critical process that relieves the stresses created during manufacturing; poor annealing reduces chemical and mechanical durability. Stones come from worn furnace refractory bricks, while phase separation and volatilization of alkali borates are undesirable effects of the high forming temperatures, not goals of annealing.
questions.reference: USP ⟨1660⟩ Formation of Molded and Tubular Glass Containers

questions.question: Which statement about treating the inner glass surface with ammonium sulfate is correct?

options.A: It converts sodium oxide to a depth of about 10-100 nm into soluble sodium sulfate that is washed away, but leaves a thin silica-rich inner surface
options.B: It converts sodium oxide to a depth of about 10-100 nm into insoluble sodium sulfate that stays on the surface, making the inner surface denser and more corrosion resistant
options.C: It can be used only on Type III glass, with the aim of raising its hydrolytic resistance to exactly that of Type I
options.D: After treatment the surface alkalinity value is reduced, so it can be ensured that the container will not delaminate with any formulation

questions.explanation: Ammonium sulfate converts sodium oxide at the surface into highly soluble sodium sulfate, which is then washed away. This lowers the tendency for pH shift but also removes structural elements, leaving a silica-rich surface layer. The process can also be applied to Type I glass, and a low surface alkalinity value does not guarantee durability, which depends on the formulation.
questions.reference: USP ⟨1660⟩ Processing of Molded and Tubular Glass Containers

questions.question: Every lot of Type I, II, or III glass containers must meet the Surface Glass Test of ⟨660⟩. What is the position of ⟨1660⟩ on this test?

options.A: It has a clear, direct correlation with glass particle formation and delamination tendency, so passing it removes the need for further screening tests
options.B: It uses the drug product itself as the extraction medium, so it reflects the actual degree of attack on the inner surface by the drug product
options.C: It applies only to molded containers; tubular glass vials have consistent surface durability and need no separate screening test
options.D: It uses water as the extraction medium and does not consider the drug product, the most important variable; it is only a first step in quality control

questions.explanation: The Surface Glass Test provides only an indication of the chemical durability of the inner surface; it has no clear, direct correlation with particle formation or delamination, and because it uses water for extraction it does not consider the drug product, which has the greatest influence. Additional screening methods are therefore needed before formal stability studies.
questions.reference: USP ⟨1660⟩ Evaluation of the Inner Surface Durability

questions.question: A product uses glass containers produced by a single supplier at several manufacturing sites. According to the recommendations of ⟨1660⟩, how should the user handle this?

options.A: As long as every lot passes the Surface Glass Test, the containers from all sites can be considered to perform identically
options.B: Rely on the supplier's glass-type certificate; differences between sites are the supplier's internal matter and need not be tracked
options.C: Obtain information to determine whether containers from the different sites perform comparably, and ensure that site differences do not significantly affect quality
options.D: Require all sites to use exactly the same ammonium sulfate treatment conditions, thereby eliminating quality differences between sites

questions.explanation: The text asks users to obtain information on the manufacturing sites in order to judge whether containers made at multiple sites perform comparably, and to ensure through the quality management plans of both parties that site differences do not significantly affect quality. The Surface Glass Test alone is not sufficient to reflect these differences.

questions.question: Which set matches the model-system conditions in Table 4 used to accelerate delamination?

options.A: 0.9% KCl pH 8.0: 24 h at 80°; 3% sodium citrate pH 8.0: 1 h at 121°
options.B: 0.9% KCl pH 8.0: 1 h at 121° (1 or 2 cycles); 3% sodium citrate pH 8.0: 24 h at 80°
options.C: 20 mM glycine pH 10.0: 1 h at 121°; 0.9% KCl pH 8.0: 24 h at 50°
options.D: 3% sodium citrate pH 8.0: 24 h at 50°; 20 mM glycine pH 10.0: 24 h at 80°

questions.explanation: The three model systems in Table 4 are: 0.9% KCl pH 8.0 at 121° for 1 h (1 or 2 cycles), 3% sodium citrate pH 8.0 at 80° for 24 h, and 20 mM glycine pH 10.0 at 50° for 24 h. The other options pair the solutions with the wrong conditions.

questions.question: A product is labeled for storage at 5°, and the appropriate accelerated condition for it is 30°. To evaluate the suitability of the glass vial for this product, what does ⟨1660⟩ recommend?

options.A: Use the 121° condition of Table 4 directly, because the harsher the condition, the more certain the vial is safe
options.B: Test at 30°, which takes only a few days and requires only a small number of samples to represent the whole lot of glass
options.C: Use the Table 4 conditions but shorten the test time, to avoid false conclusions caused by high temperature
options.D: Test at 30° over a period of weeks to months, using a larger number of vials so that the results are representative

questions.explanation: For a specific product, the accelerated conditions must be linked to conditions relevant to that product (for example, 30° for 5° storage). At the lower temperature, the test time must be extended to weeks to months, and a larger number of vials is needed. The Table 4 conditions are too aggressive and may give false positives.
questions.reference: USP ⟨1660⟩ Screening Strategy for Drug Products

questions.topic: Table 5 water control vs drug product control
questions.question: In the glass vial screening strategy of Table 5, what is the main difference between the "Water Control" and "Drug Product Control" groups?

options.A: The vials in both groups are first washed and depyrogenated and both are stored under accelerated drug product stability conditions; the difference is whether they are filled with WFI or the actual drug product
options.B: The Water Control vials are not washed or depyrogenated, whereas the Drug Product Control vials must be fully washed and depyrogenated before filling
options.C: The Water Control is filled with a stress-test solution and held at an accelerated temperature, whereas the Drug Product Control is stored under the labeled storage conditions
options.D: The Water Control needs no sterilization and no accelerated storage; only the Drug Product Control must follow the drug product stability conditions

questions.explanation: The three groups in Table 5 are Stress Test, Water Control, and Drug Product Control. The last two have the same vial handling and storage (washing, depyrogenation, autoclaving where applicable, accelerated stability conditions); only the fill differs: WFI or the actual drug product. The stress-test solution is used only in the first group.
questions.reference: USP ⟨1660⟩ Screening Strategy for Drug Products, Table 5
